Taxonomic classification depends on prefrontal regions and arrives late, while thematic classification arises earlier and depends on X

Thus, both forms of categorization-taxonomic and thematic-explain different classes of phenomena and are activated in different contexts, contributing in unique ways to cognition. The general consensus is that these two modes of conceptual organization are functionally different but complementary. This decoupling has been reported in behavioral studies (Borghi & Caramelli, 2003; Coane, McBride, Termonen, & Cutting, 2016; Landrigan & Mirman, 2018; Lin & Murphy, 2001; Masuda & Nisbett, 2001; Mirman & Graziano, 2012; Pluciennicka, Coello, & Kalenine, 2016), neuroimaging studies (Chen et al., 2013, Lewis, Poeppel, & Murphy, 2015; Sachs, Weis, Krings, Huber, & Kircher, 2008; Schwartz et al., 2011), and neuropsychological studies (Davidoff & Roberson, 2004; Kalenine, Mirman, & Buxbaum, 2012). The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Retrosplenial cortex (a subregion of the posterior cingulate cortex; responsible for egocentric-allocentric transforms), a transmodal hub sitting atop the principal gradient, has likely benefited from its input regions finally maturing/stabilizing and has now begun to mature itself, along with other higher-order, transmodal regions; for example, the emergence of reliable class inclusion marks the growing maturity of the anterior temporal cortex, which must integrate disparate object-centric information (e.g visual appearance, tactile memories, tool-use memories) to provide a full characterization of objects.

Neuroimaging studies by Houdé et al. (2011) reveal that 9-10-year-old conservers show bilateral parietofrontal network activation, particularly in the right inferior frontal gyrus associated with inhibitory control, while 5-6-year-old non-conservers show no such activation 1.

Looking closely at frontal activity, Jonkman (2006) found a linear increase in no-go P3 amplitude (a positive wave 300 - 500 ms after stimulus presentation) across development: Children ages 6-7 showed no P3 activity, children ages 9-10 showed limited P3 activity in frontal-central electrodes, and young adults showed broad P3 activity across frontal and frontal-central electrodes (see also Jonkman el al., 2003). P3 activity has been interpreted to index the allocation of attentional resources during stimulus engagement, with greater activity representing greater resource allocation (Polich, 1987). In contrast, the no-go N2 response (a negative wave 150 - 400 ms after stimulus presentation) decreased across the same age span, with the largest decrease in amplitude occurring between ages 6 and 10.

Complementing these behavioral gains, EEG studies using child-friendly flanker paradigms report more differentiated N2/P3 signatures of conflict detection and resolution by this window, consistent with a more reliable recruitment of control when distractors must be filtered 2
